scenes.narration: A function name, without brackets, is a value. You can tie it to another name, put it in a list, or pass it to another function. Brackets mean, call it now. No brackets means, here is the function itself. Think of a chef handing a recipe card to an assistant. The card is passed around, and the cooking happens only when someone follows it. A function that takes or returns functions is called higher order.

scenes.narration: [HL 1] Apply takes a function and a value. [HL 2] It calls the function on the value. [HL 3] Double. [HL 4] Returns n times two. [HL 5] Square. [HL 6] Returns n times n. [HL 7] We pass double, with no brackets. Python gives it to apply, which calls it with five. Ten. [HL 8] Pass square instead, and the same apply gives twenty five. The behaviour is now a choice we make at the call.

scenes.onScreen: Two cards: double (the function itself, handed over) and double(5) (the answer 10)
scenes.animation: A function card slides to another box; a second card with brackets turns into a number
scenes.narration: Here is the distinction. Double, with no brackets, is the function itself, a card you can hand to someone. Double of five, with brackets, is the result of running it, the number ten. Passing and calling are different things. When a function wants a function, hand over the card. Do not run it first.

lines: Passing and calling are different things.

scenes.onScreen: compose.py: make_adder returns a new function
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 1] A function that takes k. [HL 2] Inside, another function, add. [HL 3] It adds x and k. It remembers k from the outer function. [HL 4] We return add itself, with no brackets. [HL 5] Calling make adder with five gives back a new function, tied to add five. [HL 6] Add five of ten is fifteen. [HL 7] Or call twice in one line. Make adder one, then call it with one. Two.

code.source:
def make_adder(k):
    def add(x):
        return x + k
    return add
add5 = make_adder(5)
print(add5(10))
print(make_adder(1)(1))

scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We wrote double with brackets. That calls double right now, with no number. Python says, type error, double is missing one required positional argument, n. We wanted to hand over the function, not run it. Remove the brackets, and apply receives the function itself.

shorts.title: Functions are values
shorts.hook: "In Python, a function is a value, like a number or a string."
shorts.script: In Python, a function is a value, like a number or a string. Write the name without brackets, and you have the function itself. You can tie it to another name, put it in a list, or pass it to another function. This is the idea behind map, filter, and sorted with a key. It makes your code flexible, because behaviour becomes a choice. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: A function is a value.

shorts.title: Passing versus calling
shorts.script: Brackets make all the difference. Double, with no brackets, is the function itself, like a recipe card. Double of five, with brackets, runs the recipe, and gives the number ten. When another function wants a function, hand over the card. Do not run it first. Most errors in this topic come from adding brackets where they do not belong. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Card or cooked dish?

shorts.title: Return a function
shorts.hook: "A function can build and return another function."
shorts.script: A function can build and return another function. Make adder takes k, and defines a small function add, which uses k. It returns add itself. Make adder of five gives you a function that adds five. The inner function remembers k, even after make adder has finished. That memory is called a closure. It is a neat way to make custom tools. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Build a tool.

shorts.title: Missing argument
shorts.script: Here is the bug. You write apply, open bracket, double, empty brackets, comma, five. Those empty brackets call double right now, without a number. Python says, type error, double is missing one required positional argument. You meant to pass the function, not run it. Remove the brackets, and apply gets the function it asked for. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Drop the brackets.

shorts.title: Pun and challenge
shorts.hook: "Why did the function pass the baton?"
shorts.script: Why did the function pass the baton? It believed in teamwork. Your challenge. Write a function called apply twice. It takes a function f and a value x. It returns f of f of x. Then write a function that adds three. Call apply twice with it, and ten. You should see sixteen. Share your solution in the comments below. Keep coding, says Xecxec! Full video: EP 49.
shorts.caption: Try passing functions.
